abstract.title: Summary
abstract.p: Isolating human MEK/ERK signaling-independent pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) with naive pluripotency characteristics while maintaining differentiation competence and (epi)genetic integrity remains challenging. Here, we engineer reporter systems that allow the screening for defined conditions that induce molecular and functional features of human naive pluripotency. Synergistic inhibition of WNT/β-CATENIN, protein kinase C (PKC), and SRC signaling consolidates the induction of teratoma-competent naive human PSCs, with the capacity to differentiate into trophoblast stem cells (TSCs) and extraembryonic naive endodermal (nEND) cells in vitro. Divergent signaling and transcriptional requirements for boosting naive pluripotency were found between mouse and human. P53 depletion in naive hPSCs increased their contribution to mouse-human cross-species chimeric embryos upon priming and differentiation. Finally, MEK/ERK inhibition can be substituted with the inhibition of NOTCH/RBPj, which induces alternative naive-like hPSCs with a diminished risk for deleterious global DNA hypomethylation. Our findings set a framework for defining the signaling foundations of human naive pluripotency.

abstract.p: Engineered systems were used to screen for conditions that enable robust induction of human naive PSCs without the obligation for exogenous transgenes or feeder cells. The latter allowed defining the signaling and transcriptional foundations of human naive PSCs with enhanced (epi)genetic stability and competence for differentiation into all lineages.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Conventional human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) retain a variety of epigenetic properties that are consistent with possessing a primed pluripotent state. These include an inability to tolerate MEK/ERK inhibition (MEKi/ERKi), predominant utilization of the proximal enhancer element to maintain OCT4 expression, X-chromosome inactivation, and high levels of DNA methylation (Weinberger et al., 2016). Several groups have previously established conditions for deriving naive MEK/ERK signaling-independent genetically unmodified human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs). For example, naive human stem cell medium (NHSM) conditions do not require the use of exogenous transgenes or feeder cells, maintain teratoma formation competence, and contain the following components: 2iLIF, P38i/JNKi, protein kinase C inhibitor (PKCi), ROCKi, ACTIVIN, and FGF2 (Gafni et al., 2013). Under NHSM conditions, hPSCs exhibit some naive features, most notably pluripotency preservation while MEK/ERK signaling is inhibited, which is the hallmark of mammalian naive pluripotency (Takashima et al., 2014), predominant TFE3 nuclear localization, in vitro reconstitution of human primordial germ cells (PGCs), and a mild reduction in DNA methylation (Gafni et al., 2013; Irie et al., 2015). The latter effect is profoundly weaker than the one observed in mouse pluripotent cells, suggesting sub-optimal human naive pluripotency growth conditions.

Alternative conditions that generate MEK-independent human naive cells and that retain a more compelling milieu of naive transcriptional markers were developed. Several components found in NHSM (2i, PKCi, ROCKi, ACTIVIN, FGF2) were supplemented with BRAF inhibitors to generate mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF)-dependent naive cell lines (termed 5iLA) (Theunissen et al., 2014). Globally, these conditions generated more pronounced downregulation in DNA methylation and upregulation of naive pluripotent cell markers. However, the hypomethylation under these conditions was accompanied by immediate and global loss of imprinting over all imprinted loci (Bar et al., 2017; Pastor et al., 2016) and confounding chromosomal abnormalities in nearly all lines generated within only 10 passages (Liu et al., 2017). Derivation of naive hESCs in t2iL-Go (or t2iL-GoY), a combination of small molecules included within our previous NHSM transgene-free conditions (Gafni et al., 2013), has been reported with the use of exogenous NANOG-KLF2 transgenes induction, yet the generated cell lines were not shown thus far to robustly form teratomas in vivo and can differentiate in vitro only after an extended 3-week transfer into primed conditions (Guo et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017; Takashima et al., 2014). The latter is in striking difference from rodent naive PSCs, which can initiate differentiation in vivo following cell autonomous induction of the needed priming or formative capacitating signals toward differentiation (Ying et al., 2008).

Collectively, these prior studies suggest that none of the conditions devised so far is optimal or can reduce the gap between mouse and human naive pluripotency characteristics. In this study, we set out to devise enhanced conditions that enable the stabilization of hPSCs with stringent naive functional and molecular properties while preserving cell-autonomous differentiation competence into embryonic, germ cell and extra-embryonic lineages. This was complemented by efforts to decipher the features of signaling and regulatory circuitry of such naive PSCs. Simultaneously, we aimed to establish robust defined conditions that do not require the obligatory use of exogenous transgenes, broad histone deacytelase inhibitors or feeder cells to induce human naive pluripotency.

sec.title: Defining human naive pluripotency conditions that endow tolerance for depletion of RNA/DNA methylation
sec.p:
Recent studies have defined the functional ability of 2i/LIF conditions to maintain mouse naive pluripotency upon knocking out epigenetic repressors like Mettl3 and Dnmt1 (m6A mRNA and DNA methyltransferase enzymes, respectively), while epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs) differentiate and undergo apoptosis upon the complete ablation of the same factors (Geula et al., 2015; Liao et al., 2015). These noted functional differences led us to hypothesize that they might be utilized to screen and define the conditions that endow this stringent naive pluripotency feature (i.e., maintenance of pluripotency in the absence of defined epigenetic repressors). We engineered WIBR3 hESC lines with inducible ablation of METTL3 expression (Figures 1A and 1B). Primed Tet-OFF-METTL3 hESCs expanded in primed conditions could not be sustained in the presence of DOX (Figure 1C). In the presence of MEFs, Tet-OFF-METTL3 could be poorly maintained in previously described NHSM conditions, but not in other previously described naive conditions (Figures 1C, S1A, and S1B). However, in the absence of MEFs, NHSM conditions also could not support the maintenance of pluripotency when METTL3 was ablated. We thus set out to test candidate molecules that may enrich NHSM conditions and allow the maintenance of Tet-OFF-METTL3 cells on DOX.Figure 1

We tested whether supplementing NHSM with various small molecules previously implicated in boosting naive pluripotency formation or induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derivation efficiency might achieve this goal (Figure 1D). Remarkably, adding the small molecule IWR1 enabled the expansion of Tet-OFF-METTL3 hESCs on DOX (Figure 1E). IWR1 is a WNT inhibitor (WNTi) that stabilizes the AXIN protein in the cytoplasm by inhibiting the Tankyrase enzyme (TNKi). Adding to the NHSM an independent specific TNKi, XAV939, yielded a similar effect (Figure 1F). Notably, a number of recent publications have included TNKi among other ingredients for generating naive, extended potential, or primed PSCs (Smith et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2017a, 2017b; Zimmerlin et al., 2016). However, none of these reported conditions could maintain OCT4+ in the absence of METTL3 or DNMT1 (Figures S1A and S1B), likely due to the absence of other key ingredients synergistically used in NHSM conditions but not in these previously described conditions.

We used ΔPE-OCT4-GFP naive pluripotency reporter lines (Theunissen et al., 2014) (Figure S1C) and found that supplementation of TNKi to NHSM conditions yielded an increase in GFP (Figures 1G and S1C). Consistent with studies conducted in mice (Kim et al., 2013), adding TNKi rendered exogenous supplementation of FGF2 dispensable (Figure 1G). Further, as TNKi inhibits WNT signaling, we validated that including GSK3 inhibitor (GSK3i) is dispensable and, in fact, compromises the intensity of naive ΔPE-OCT4-GFP signal (Figure S1D). Although dispensable, JNK/P38 inhibition boosted naive pluripotency marker expression and cell viability and, therefore, was included in the induction media used herein as an optional secondary booster (Figure S1E).

sec.title: Defining human naive pluripotency conditions independent of exogenous TGF/ACTIVIN
sec.p:
When induced under NHSM conditions with the above modifications, hESCs maintained uniformly high ΔPE-OCT4-GFP levels only in the presence of exogenous ACTIVIN A and differentiated when transforming growth factor (TGF) receptor (TGFR) inhibitor was introduced (Figures 1H, 1I, and S1F). We employed a second targeted screening strategy in an effort to identify a small molecule whose addition to NHSM generates hPSCs without the need for exogenous ACTIVIN supplementation. To do this, candidate molecules were added to NHSM conditions supplemented with TNKi but lacking ACTIVIN A to screen for OCT4+ PSCs that are induced independently of METTL3 expression (on DOX) (Figure 2A). While in most conditions OCT4+ cell fraction rapidly deteriorated, a SRC inhibitor (SRCi = CGP77675) maintained the stability of dome-like OCT4+ cells (Figure 2B). The latter led us to assemble a defined FGF/TGF/ACTIVIN/MEF-independent and serum-free condition termed human enhanced naive stem cell medium (HENSM) (Figures 2C–2E). Supplementation of SRCi and Geltrex in ACTIVIN-A-containing media, although not essential, supported the consistency of a dome-like morphology among naive cells and boosted naive marker expression (Figures S1G and S1H) (termed HENSM-ACT).Figure 2

hESCs maintained their dome-like morphology and expressed naive pluripotency marker KLF17 in HENSM (Figure S2A). The cells generated mature teratomas without the need to passage them first in primed conditions prior to their injection (Figure 2F). To extend the previous findings to other repressor machineries, DGCR8 null cells were expanded in HENSM and retained expression of naive ΔPE-OCT4-GFP reporter (Figure S2B). To test which of the naive conditions enables expanding naive hPSCs in the absence of DNMT1, primed TET-OFF DNMT1 hESCs (Figure 2G) (Liao et al., 2015) were transferred into previously described naive conditions including NHSM, 5i/LA. t2iL-GO, and TESR/3iL-MEF and could not be maintained in the presence of DOX (Figures 2H and 2I). Strikingly, HENSM and HENSM-ACT conditions allowed stable induction, and unlimited expansion of DNMT1 depleted human OCT4+ ESCs (Figure 2I). Collectively, these results demonstrate that HENSM conditions closely mimic stringent characteristics of mouse naive ESCs and enable generation of hPSCs ablated for epigenetic repressors.

As shown previously for naive hPSCs in NHSM, 5i-LA, and t2iL-Go (Sperber et al., 2015), HENSM conditions also increase their oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) activity (Figure S2C). A newly identified metabolic feature in naive ESCs in 2i/LIF is that they can endogenously synthesize glutamine at sufficient levels to maintain adequate alpha-ketogluterate (αKG) levels (Carey et al., 2015). While they benefit from exogenous L-glutamine supplementation, it is not essential for their stability, as they can endogenously synthesize it. Primed EpiSCs cannot be maintained in the absence of exogenous L-glutamine for an extended period (Carey et al., 2015). hESC lines were then tested for the ability to induce naive pluripotency in the presence and absence of exogenously added L-glutamine (Figure 2J). We failed to maintain primed PSCs or induce naivety in previously described naive conditions in the absence of L-glutamine (Figure 2J), while cells in HENSM obtained naive pluripotency even in the absence of exogenous L-glutamine (Figure S2D).

sec.title: Transcriptional characterization of hPSCs in HENSM conditions
sec.p: We established five new hESC lines from blastocysts (LIS36, LIS42, and LIS46 in HENSM-ACT and LIS41 and LIS49 ESCs in HENSM). Human dermal fibroblast or blood cells were reprogrammed into iPSCs in HENSM conditions. hESC and hiPSC lines expanded in HENSM conditions were positive for pluripotency markers (OCT4, NANOG, SSEA4, TRA1-60, TRA1-81, STELLA, DNMT3L, TFCP2L1, and KLF17) (Figure S2E); formed mature teratomas (Figure S2F); and differentiated, without a need for in vitro priming, directly into bona fide extra-embryonic trophoblast stem cells (TSCs) (Figure S2G) and extra-embryonic naive primitive endoderm cells (PrE and nEND cells) (Figures S2H and S2I) (Linneberg-Agerholm et al., 2019; Okae et al., 2018). Naive hPSC lines were passaged with TryplE every 4–5 days and maintained robust growth (Figure S2J). Naive hPSCs maintained normal karyotype after extended passaging in HENSM-ACT or HENSM in most lines tested (Figure S2K). This indicates that epigenetic resetting in HENSM does not cause obligatory chromosomal abnormalities or select for pre-existing abnormal variants, as has been seen for other naive conditions like 5iLA-MEF or t2iL-Go (Liu et al., 2017).

Unbiased clustering of genome-wide expression profiles demonstrated that naive hESCs and hiPSCs possess a distinct gene expression pattern and cluster separately from primed hPSCs (Figures 3A and 3B). Transcripts associated with naive pluripotency were significantly upregulated in naive cells, including NANOG, TFCP2L1, KLF17, KLF4, STELLA (DPPA3), DPPA5, DNMT3L, KHDC1L, and ARGFX (Figures 3C and S3A; Tables S1, S2, and S3). ESRRB, previously purported to be a regulator of human naive pluripotency (Takashima et al., 2014), was not detectable in the cells described herein, consistent with its lack of expression in human ICM (Petropoulos et al., 2016). Naive pluripotent cells had downregulated lineage commitment genes like T, OTX2, ZIC2, and VIM1 (Figure S3B; Table S1). When including previously published naive datasets generated in 5iLA and t2iL-Go, we note that cells generated in HENSM and HENSM-ACT conditions clustered with the latter naive conditions and not with primed samples (Figures 3A and 3B). Similar transcriptional qualities were detected in hPSCs expanded in HENSM Xeno-free (HENSM-XF conditions) on BioLaminin511-coated plates (Figure 3A). SUSD2 surface marker was expressed on all naive lines tested; however, it was meaningfully expressed on nearly 50% of human primed cell lines (Figure S3D), which provides a cautionary note regarding recent claims that it is an exclusive marker for naive PSCs (Bredenkamp et al., 2019b). Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) analysis confirmed the upregulation of previously identified human naive pluripotency markers Gb3/CD77 and IL6ST/CD130 in HENSM conditions, and primed pluripotency marker CD24 was downregulated (Figure S3E) (Collier et al., 2017). By comparing the transcriptome to that described during early human pre-implantation development, cells expanded in HENSM and 5iLA conditions, but not primed cells, showed specific enrichment to profiles of late morula-early blastocyst-specific signature (Figure 3D). Similar to their importance in maintaining human naive pluripotency in 5i/LA conditions (Pastor et al., 2018), TFAP2C knockout (KO) lines showed that it is essential for naive hPSC expansion in HENSM conditions (Figure S3C).Figure 3

sec.title: Epigenetic characterization of hPSCs in HENSM conditions
sec.p: We explored change in chromatin accessibility of each condition by ATAC-seq and compared it to unique chromatin accessibility loci found in different pre-implantation stages. We compared how many of these loci show an increase or decrease in chromatin accessibility of naive compared to primed hESCs. Like in datasets generated in 5iLA-MEF and t2iL-Go-MEF, HENSM hESC chromatin accessibility corresponds more to the ICM than to earlier stages (Figure 3E). These results support the endowment of late pre-implantation like transposon expression (Table S4) and chromatin accessibility profile in PSCs expanded in HENSM conditions.

We next tested whether HENSM conditions endow naive hPSCs with a pre-X-chromosome configuration. We used WIBR2 hESCs carrying knockin MECP2-tdTomato and MECP2-GFP alleles (Figure 4A) (Theunissen et al., 2016). Upon transferring the primed cells for five passages into HENSM conditions, >88% of cells expressed both fluorescent markers, consistent with reactivation of both X chromosomes. Transferring early passage cells back into primed media allowed inactivation of the X chromosome, as evident by obtaining GFP-/tdTomato+ pattern in >95% of the reprimed cells in a non-random manner (Figure 4A). Consistent with a recent report emphasizing the importance of FGFR signaling inhibition to generate cells with ability for random X inactivation (An et al., 2020), extended passaging in HENSM or supplementing HENSM conditions with FGFRi or increasing ERKi concentration generated naive hPSCs capable of random X inactivation upon priming (Figures S3F and S3G).Figure 4

We sampled naive hPSCs for DNA methylation status by whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS). Lines tested displayed a profound downregulation of global methylation levels (Figures 4B and 4C), from ∼81% in primed hPSCs to ∼55% in HENSM-ACT and to ∼66% in HENSM expanded hPSCs. It has been previously shown in mouse naive conditions that rapid loss of global DNA methylation level results from a partial decrease in UHRF1 protein expression levels while maintaining DNMT1 levels (von Meyenn et al., 2016). In human cells expanded in HENSM, DNMT1 methyltransferase protein expression is maintained, while UHRF1 protein is partially depleted (Figure 4D), which may underlie the global downregulation in DNA methylation in HENSM conditions. Supplementing HENSM with BRAF inhibitor used in 5i/LAF conditions leads to dramatic downregulation in DNMT1 as well (Figure 2H) and might explain the immediate and global loss of imprinting seen in 5iLA conditions (Pastor et al., 2016). As DNMT1 levels are maintained in HENSM conditions, and UHRF1 protein downregulation was partial, we did not observe immediate global loss of all imprinted genes in HENSM conditions (Figure S3H), contrary to what has been previously seen in 5iLA or t2iL-Go (Pastor et al., 2016; Theunissen et al., 2016). However, loss of imprinting in HENSM occurred sporadically only at some individual loci, at lower frequencies, and only after prolonged cell passaging (Figure S3H), which constitutes an improvement over previously reported hypomethylated naive hPSCs.

sec.title: Differentiation competence of naive hiPSCs following interspecies chimerism in mice
sec.p: Given that the naive hPSCs described above maintained genetic integrity and were capable of forming teratomas, we moved to evaluate whether naive hiPSCs can integrate and differentiate following microinjection into host mouse blastocysts (Gafni et al., 2013). NHSM- and HENSM-derived hiPSCs were able to colonize mouse embryos up to E17.5 at various anatomic regions of different embryonic germ layers (Figures S4A and S4B). Immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining of chimeric embryos confirmed a distinct expression of various developmental compartments, including markers found in murine lungs on GFP+ derived human cells (Figure S4C).

Our results indicate that the contribution levels of human GFP+ cells in mouse embryos, although meaningful and reproducible, are relatively low (∼3% of mice are chimeric with naive hiPSC-derived cells). Thus, we sought to develop technical platforms that can enhance such integration and allow us to better visualize integrating human cells in the developing mouse embryo. Mouse ESCs depleted for p53 outcompete host pluripotent cells after blastocyst microinjection by a cell competition phenomenon that has been recently documented in mice (Dejosez et al., 2013), and can generate very high contribution chimeras. Thus, we tested whether manipulating these pathways might similarly endow injected naive hiPSCs expanded in NHSM or HENSM conditions, with a cross-species competitive advantage and increase human cell chimerism in developing mouse embryos. Remarkably, after microinjection of P53-depleted hPSCs into mouse morulas or aggregation with 2-cell embryos, a 4-fold increase in the number of chimeric animals was obtained (Figures 4e and S4C–S4F) as well as an increase in the extent of chimerism per embryo (Figures 4e and S4D–S4F). Differentiation was validated in chimeric embryos for major developmental markers, covering all embryonic germ layers overlapping extensively with human-derived GFP signal (Figures 4F and S5). These results substantiate the generation of advanced human-mouse interspecies chimera with various engraftment in defined lineages up to E17.5 from both NHSM and HENSM conditions.

sec.title: WNT/β-CATENIN signaling is a major inhibitor of human naive pluripotency induction
sec.p:
Functional naive pluripotency induction in HENSM composition relies not only on inhibition of ERK and PKC pathways, but also on inhibition of TNK and SRC (Figures 5A and 5B). We next aimed to define the signaling pathway downstream of TNKi that facilitates naive hPSCs stabilization. WNT signaling is a well-established promoter of rodent naive pluripotency; it leads to β-CATENIN (βCAT) nuclear localization, which, in turn, neutralizes the repression by TCF3 effector and derepresses naive pluripotency targets (ten Berge et al., 2011; Wray et al., 2011). Although some studies have indicated that moderating the WNT stimulation level is needed when generating human naive cells using lower doses of GSK3i or by simultaneously adding TNKi and GSK3i (leading to high cytoplasmic βCAT) (Theunissen et al., 2014; Zimmerlin et al., 2016), they concluded that WNT stimulation is helpful for promoting human naive pluripotency exactly as seen in mouse PSCs. Other studies indicated that WNTi is beneficial for the initial reversion of primed to naive pluripotency (Bredenkamp et al., 2019a); however, it was suggested that inclusion of 2i with WNT stimulation is equally optimal for maintaining naive hPSCs (Bredenkamp et al., 2019b; Guo et al., 2017).Figure 5

Given that prior studies did not rely on exacting reporter and KO models for WNT signaling, we generated βCAT KO cells on naive pluripotency reporter lines to give a definitive answer to this question. βCAT-KO hESCs maintained high levels of ΔPE-OCT4-GFP in HENSM conditions, and upon removal of TNKi, the GFP level was not decreased in βCAT-KO, only in wild-type (WT) ESCs (Figure 5C). Supplementing naive cells with WNT stimulator, like CHIR99021 (CHIR), or depleting TNKi activated WNT signaling in hPSCs (Figure 5D), compromised their domed shape morphology (Figure 5E) and their naive transcriptional profile (Figure 3A). We introduced tamoxifen-induced βCAT-ERT transgene into βCAT-KO hESCs and noted that in human ΔPE-OCT4-GFP signal, naive transcription profile and domed morphology were compromised upon 4OHT stimulation (Figures 5F, 5G, and S6A). This is in striking contrast to mouse ESCs that, upon tamoxifen treatment, induced naive characteristic domed like morphology and markers (Figure 5F). Similarly, while KO of Tcf3 boosts mouse naive pluripotency and alleviates the need for WNT stimulation (Wray et al., 2011), TCF3 KO hESCs (Figures 5E and S6B) still required WNTi to acquire their naive identity upon transitioning into HENSM. Supplementing HENSM with CHIR compromised their ability to induce pluripotency upon depletion of DNA and RNA methylation or omitting L-glutamine from the culture conditions (Figure S6C). Cross-species comparison of in vivo mouse and human RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data of pre-implantation blastocysts shows a strong signature for AXIN1/2 upregulation in human but not mouse ICM (Figure S6D). Naive hPSCs express profound levels of several WNT ligands (Figure 5H), and Porcupine inhibitor IWP2, which abrogates WNT ligand secretion, replaced TNKi in HENSM conditions and enabled generating naive hPSCs (Figures 5I and 5J). Collectively, these findings establish WNT-βCAT signaling as a major priming agent for human, but not mouse, naive pluripotency and establish that ablation of βCAT can substitute for the need for TNKi or WNTi.

The results of ΔPE-OCT4-GFP, pluripotency gene expression, and DNA hypomethylation establish that ACTIVIN A supports human naive pluripotency (Figures 1H, 3C, 4B, and 4C). The latter can be consistent with the observations that single-cell RNA-seq data on mouse and human ICMs show that human ICM retains high NODAL expression, but not that of BMP4, which is highly expressed in the mouse ICM (Blakeley et al., 2015; Weinberger et al., 2016). Although not compulsory, supplementation of ACTIVIN A during initial phases of primed to naive reversion greatly enhances efficiency of naive PSC clone recovery both in feeder-containing and feeder-free conditions. Later, ACTIVIN A concentration can be tapered down or completely omitted. In mouse naive conditions, LIF/Stat3 has been shown to be a booster for naive marker expression; however, it can be omitted without the entire collapse of the naive state (Ying et al., 2008). By omitting LIF from HENSM conditions and by generating STAT3 KO naive hPSCs, we show that LIF can boost naive marker expression (Figure S6E); however, it can be dispensable for human cells, too (Figure S6F).

sec.title: KLF17 is important for human, but not mouse, naive pluripotency induction
sec.p:
Analysis of chromatin accessibility revealed differences in accessibility of DNA binding proteins and protein families, unique for each pluripotent configuration. Binding motifs of different transcription factors (TFs) like KLF17 and KLF4 were found to be significantly enriched (corrected p value ∼0) in naive chromatin accessible loci, whereas those in the GATA family are more prone to be found in the primed condition (Figure 6A; Table S5). P53 signature was very prominent in human naive and ICM (Figure S6H) and might explain why p53 depletion enhances chimerism with human cells (Figure 4E), consistent with a recent report published while this paper was in revision (Zheng et al., 2021).Figure 6

We initially focused on the KLF17 gene, which is specifically expressed in human naive conditions. We generated single- and double-primed KO ESC lines for KLF4 and KLF17 TFs. Remarkably KO of KLF17 led to a collapse of naive pluripotency in HENSM, and HENSM-ACT cells showed notable differentiation (62% OCT4-GFP+ cells) and a slower growth rate (Figure 6B), indicating that ACTIVIN A cannot fully compensate for the loss of KLF17. Double-KO ESCs for KLF4/KLF17 deteriorated toward differentiation, and most cells lost OCT4-GFP expression upon reversion in both HENSM and HENSM-ACT conditions (Figure 6B). In mice, Klf17 is not expressed in the mouse ICM or ESCs, but rather in the 4-cell stage in vivo (Figure S6G). Klf17 KO mice were viable, and pups were obtained at the expected mendelian ratios. Unlike the phenotype seen in human KLF17 KO ESCs in HENSM, mouse Klf17 KO ESCs were indistinguishable from WT cells (Figures 6C and S6I). These results establish a significant dependency of human, but not mouse, naive pluripotency on KLF17.

We examined the DNA binding profile of the master pluripotent TF regulators OCT4 and SOX2 and naive promoting TFs like KLF17, KLF4, and TFAP2C by using chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq). KLF17 binds 12,197 genes, mostly in their promoter (59% are ≤1 kb from transcription start site [TSS]; Figure 6D), unlike OCT4/SOX2 that bind typically to enhancers (72% and 85% in distal intergenic regions and introns, respectively). KLF17 binds more substantially to naive-specific open regions (Figure 6E). Interestingly, OCT4 and SOX2, known to work as a complex (Merino et al., 2014), show high correlation between their binding targets, yet share significantly fewer reciprocal binding sites with other naive-specific KLF17 and KLF4 genes (Figure 6F). The latter may explain why despite the presence of OCT4 and SOX2 in naive hPSCs, these regulators could not compensate for depletion of KLF4 or KLF17, as the latter constitute major regulators of naive-pluripotency-specific genes whose genomic regulatory elements are not directly bound by OCT4 or SOX2 (e.g., KLF4, DPPA3, NODAL, HORMAD1; Figure 6G; Table S6).

sec.title: Inhibition of NOTCH/RBPj facilitates capture of human naive pluripotency without ERKi
sec.p:
In mice, using alternative naive conditions that do not employ ERKi allows isolating murine PSCs with features of naivety, except from global hypomethylation (Choi et al., 2017; Yagi et al., 2017), and thus provides a safer route for exploiting mouse naive PSCs. We thus wanted to explore whether and how it might be feasible to expand naive hPSCs without using FGFRi/ERKi. Withdrawal or partial (33%) titration of ERKi from HENSM compromised the naivety of hESCs, as evident by loss of X reactivation (Figure 7A). Thus, we set out to screen for added compounds that would enable maintenance of pre-X inactivation upon omitting or titrating MEKi/ERKi (Figure 7B). Remarkably, we noted that adding gamma secretase inhibitor DBZ, which blocks NOTCH pathway (Ichida et al., 2014), allowed robust and feeder-free induction and maintenance of human naive cells when ERKi was omitted (0HENSM conditions) or titrated down (tHENSM conditions) (Figures 7C–7F). hPSCs induced in 0HENSM and tHENSM maintained ΔPE-OCT4-GFP signal equivalent to HENSM conditions (Figure 7E) and pre-X-inactivation state in female cell lines (Figure 7C). RT-PCR analysis showed that the lines expressed naive pluripotency markers (Figure 7G), although levels were less induced in comparison to HENSM conditions. Despite the latter, global gene expression analysis showed that the cells still clustered with HENSM naive PSCs rather than with primed PSCs (Figures 7H and S7A). At the functional levels, the cells showed no enhanced tendency for obtaining chromosomal abnormalities (Figure S2K), integrated in the mouse ICM upon microinjection (Figure S7B), and were proficient in differentiating into PGCs (Figure S7C) and making teratomas (Figure S7D). Cells could be induced upon depletion of DNMT1, METTL3, or exogenous L-glutamine (Figure S7E). WGBS analysis showed that these alternative 0HENSM and tHENSM conditions did not show trends of global hypomethylation and thus did not show accelerated loss of imprinting (Figure 7I).Figure 7

Western blot analysis showed that phosphorylated ERK is not reduced in 0HENSM conditions (Figure 7J). Recently, mouse Rbpj was identified as a major repressor for mouse naive pluripotency (Kalkan et al., 2019). The use of a newly described direct inhibitor for RBPj (termed RIN1) (Hurtado et al., 2019) in HENSM conditions substituted for the effect of DBZ on human naive pluripotency (Figure 7K). We generated RBPj KO hESCs, which allowed expanding naive hPSCs in tHENSM and 0HENSM without adding DBZ, proving that RBPj (Castel et al., 2013) is the main mediator of dismantling naive pluripotency in human cells when ERKi is depleted (Figures 7L and S7F). We note that RBPj ablation led to an upregulation of naive pluripotency markers greater than that seen with gamma secretase inhibitor DBZ (Figure 7L), suggesting that RBPj might also be regulated by NOTCH independent input.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The findings reported herein consolidate the previously raised notion (Hanna et al., 2009, 2010a, 2010b) that different genetic backgrounds assume distinct states of pluripotency in vitro, the stability of which is regulated by endogenous genetic determinants that remain unknown. The stem cell state can be modified by defined exogenous factors that support the naive state of pluripotency. The stringent requirement for these exogenous factors appears to differ among distinct species, as exemplified by the requirement for a larger set of simultaneously inhibited pathways in human cells. However, the net effect of a certain pathway like WNT and ACTIVIN signaling on naive pluripotency induction is divergent between mice and humans, as WNTi and ACTIVIN stimulation promote naive pluripotency formation only in humans. Unlike in mice, the human ICM lack ESRRB, which is a major mediator of WNT activation of naive pluripotency in mice (Blakeley et al., 2015; Martello et al., 2012; Petropoulos et al., 2016). This finding might underlie the lack of evidence in our study for a positive effect of WNT signaling on human naive pluripotency. Our results also suggest that the epigenetic priming of human pluripotent cells is predominantly caused by the supplementation of WNT, TGF, and FGF.

The functional screening systems utilized herein alongside reporter systems for human naive pluripotency helped us define multiple pathways whose modulation (activation or inhibition) promotes human naive pluripotency induction (e.g., PKC inhibition, WNTi, ACTIVIN stimulation, SRCi, RBPj inhibition, alongside using FGFRi/MEKi and LIF). While these modulators can substitute for one another, such as the ability to omit ACTIVIN A when SRCi is introduced, this does not necessarily indicate that one factor (e.g., ACTIVIN A) promotes human naive pluripotency by inhibiting the other (e.g., SRCi), but rather that key human naive pluripotency factors can be redundantly influenced by multiple signaling pathways, as has been previously described in mice (Dunn et al., 2014).

We find that human naïve PSCs are more amenable to directly generate extra-embryonic cells upon direct in vitro differentiation, when compared to their murine counterparts. Further, the fact that murine naive cells, rather than primed cells, are relatively more tolerant to ablation of some epigenetic repressors supports the concept of naive pluripotency as a synthesis with a relatively minimal requirement for epigenetic repression (Geula et al., 2015). Furthermore, our results in mice and human indicate that the ability to tolerate permanent ablation of such repressors may be one of the key features of naive pluripotency across different species and might prove to be an efficient method for inducing naive pluripotency from other species in vitro.

sec.title: Limitations of study
sec.p: We cannot exclude that alternative growth conditions may capture naive hPSCs with features similar to those described herein or that modified HENSM conditions might further improve and consolidate the extent of naive features in hPSCs or reduce further the emergence of genetic and epiegentic abnormalities. It will be interesting to define in the future whether HENSM conditions could be further simplified once naive pluripotency is established. While P53 depletion in human PSCs boosted their cross-species chimeric contribuion in mouse embryos, we did not find HENSM conditions to be superior to NHSM platform in this assay. X reactivation under some of the alternative naive conditions described herein still cannot yield random inactivation upon the differentiation of hPSCs.

sec.title: Previously described human alternative naive-like and primed conditions

sec.title: HENSM conditions
sec.p: The following serum free conditions, termed HENSM (Human Enhanced Naïve Stem cell Medium) were generated by Enhancing previous described NHSM conditions (Gafni et al., 2013) and used to isolate, generate, derive and stabilize naive human pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs and ESCs) with the unique biological properties described in this study.

HENSM medium: 240 mL Neurobasal (ThermoFisher 21103049) and 240 mL of DMEM-F12 without HEPES (ThermoFisher 21331020), 5 mL N2 supplement (ThermoFisher 17502048 or in-house prepared), 5 mL GlutaMAX (ThermoFisher 35050061), 1% nonessential amino acids (BI 01-340-1B), 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin (BI 03-031-1B), 10 mL B27 supplement (Invitrogen 17504-044 or in-house made), 0.8 mM Dimethyl 2-oxoglutarate (aKG) (add 60 μL from purchased solution from Sigma 349631), Geltrex (Invitrogen A1413202/A1413302 - add 1 mL rapidly in media to obtain 0.2% final conc), 50 μg/ml Vitamin C (L-Ascorbic acid 2-phosphate sesquimagnesium salt hydrate - Sigma A8950), 20 ng/ml recombinant human LIF (Peprotech 300-05) and the following small molecule inhibitors: FGFRi/MEKi/ERKi (PD0325901 1 μM - Axon Medchem 1408); WNTi/TNKi (XAV939 2μM – Sigma X3004 or Axon Medchem 1527); , PKCi (Go6983 2μM - Axon Medchem 2466), SRCi (CGP77675 1.2μM – Axon Medchem 2097). Secondary boosting optional components: P38i/JNKi (BIRB0796 0.8μM - Axon Medchem 1358), ROCKi Y27632 (1.2 μM - Axon Medchem 1683), and ACTIVIN A (ACT) as detailed below.
For HENSM-ACT, the latter HENSM conditions were supplemented with 5-20 ng/ml recombinant human ACTIVIN A (Peprotech 120-14E).
For 0HENSM conditions – PD0325901 was omitted and replaced with DBZ (0.15-0.3 μM – TOCRIS 4489).
For tHENSM conditions titrate concentration of ERKI were used (0.33microM PD0325901 - Axon Medchem 1408) together with DBZ (0.15 μM – TOCRIS 4489).

For Xeno FREE HENSM conditions we used Xeno Free B27 supplement (Thermo- A148670) and Xeno Free CTS N2 supplement (Thermo - A1370701). Geltrex was omitted from the medium. Cells were expanded on Biolaminin-511 (LN511-Biolamina) coated plates.
For HENSM conditions based on IWP2 – 2μM of IWP2 (TOCRIS 3533) was used instead of TNKi (XAV939).
For 0HENSM conditions based on RIN1 – 0.5μM of RIN1 (RBPj inhibitor, AXON Medchem 3061) was used instead of NOTCHi (DBZ).

Cells in HENSM were grown on 1% Growth factor reduced Matrigel (BD FAL356231) or 1% GELTREX (ThermoFisher A1413202 or A1413302) or Biolaminin-511 (Biolamina Inc; including for HENSM-XF conditions) coated plates for at least 1 hour in 37°C. Notably, coated plates with 0.2% gelatin and irradiated ICR-DR4 MEFs can also be used to maintain human naive cells in HENSM conditions. Enhanced single cell cloning efficiency can be obtained with HENSM supplementation with additional 5μM of Y-27632 ROCKi for 24 hours after cell passaging. TrypLE (ThermoFisher 12604013 or 12604054) (diluted into 0.5X - EDTA 0.75mM) is optimal for single cell passaging (2 mL per 10cm dish, 0.75 mL per 6 well - for 5 min at 37°C). After removal of TrypLE and air-drying at RT for 3 min., cells are resuspended in PBS. Rapid 0.05% trypsinization (0.5-1 min at 37C) is optimal for passaging as small clumps. Longer 0.05% trypsinization for 3-5 minutes at 37°C is optimal for microinjection into as the cells come out less sticky. Harvested cells should be centrifuged for 4 min x 1300RPM. Cells were expanded in 5% O2 and 5% CO2 conditions and passaged every 4-5 days. Medium was freshly replaced every 24 hours. Assembled media can be used for up to 7 days after preparation if kept at 4C. Passage numbers of naive-hiPSC/hESCs indicate number of passages counted after induction or stabilization of the naive state (and do not include previous passages when the cells were established and maintained in other conditions). Where indicated FGFRi 173074 (0.5-0.75 μM) was added to HENSM conditions. Where indicated, HENSM extra ERKi conditions contained 1.25 μM of PD0325901 ERKi (instead of standard 1 μM PD032590 concentration). Most efficient and rapid reversion of primed conditions into HENSM naive platform, can be performed in HENSM-ACT condition with or without MEF cells for 5 passages, after which ACTIVIN A can be omitted or tapered down. Most efficient and rapid reversion of primed conditions into 0HENSM naive platform, can be performed in 0HENSM-ACT condition with or without MEF cells for 5 passages, after which ACTIVIN A can be omitted or tapered down.

For transfection of mouse and human naive iPSCs/ESCs, 10 million cells were harvested with 0.05% trypsin-EDTA solution (Invitrogen), and cells resuspended in PBS+/+ were transfected with 100-150 μg DNA constructs (Gene Pulser Xcell System; Bio- Rad; 220V, 25 μF, square wave, 20 ms, 4 mm cuvettes). Cell lines were monthly checked for Mycoplasma contaminations (LONZA – MYCOALERT KIT), and all samples analyzed in this study were not contaminated. Instead of adding 5 mL of commercially available N2 supplements, individual components can be added to 500 mL media bottle at the indicated final concentrations: 1) Recombinant Human Insulin (Sigma I-1882) – 12.5 μg/ml final concentration; 2) Apo-Transferrin (Sigma T-1147) – 500 μg/ml final concentration; 3) Progesterone (Sigma P8783) – 0.02 μg/ml final concentration; 4) Putrescine (Sigma P5780) – 16 μg/ml final concentration; 5) Sodium Selenite (Sigma S5261) - add 5 μL of 3 mM stock solution per 500 mL HENSM media.

sec.title: Culture of conventional primed human ESCs and iPSCs
sec.p: The following already established conventional human ESCs and iPSC lines were used (indicated passage number of the cell line taken for conversion into naive pluripotency is indicated in parentheses): Human induced pluripotent stem cells C1 (P25) hiPSC lines and the human embryonic stem cell (hESC) lines H1 (P42), H9 (P39), WIBR1 (P51), WIBR2 (P44), WIBR3 (P42), HUES64, LIS1, WIS1, LIS2 hESCs were maintained in 5% O2 conditions (unless indicated otherwise) on irradiated mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) feeder layers or Matrigel coated plates as indicated. Two conventional and established conditions were used as indicated throughout the figures and manuscript: TeSR conditions on Matrigel coated plates (Stem Cell Technologies) or FGF/KSR conditions on MEF substrate: DMEM-F12 (Invitrogen 10829) supplemented with 15% Knockout Serum Replacement (Invitrogen 10828-028), 1mM GlutaMAX (Invitrogen), 1% nonessential amino acids (Invitrogen), 1% Sodium-pyruvate (BI 03-042-1B), 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin (BI 03-031-1B), 0.1 mM β-mercaptoethanol (Sigma), and 8 ng/mL bFGF (Peprotech) and 2 ng/ml recombinant human TGFβ1 (Peprotech). Cultures were passaged every 5–7 days either manually or by trypsinization (24 hours pre and 24 hours after addition of ROCK inhibitor at 5-10μM concentration). For transfection of hiPSC and hESC lines, cells were cultured in Rho kinase (ROCK) inhibitor (Y27632) 24 h before electroporation. Primed human ESC and iPSC cells were harvested with 0.05% trypsin-EDTA solution (Invitrogen), and cells resuspended in PBS were transfected with 75-100 μg DNA constructs (Gene Pulser Xcell System; Bio- Rad; 250 V, 500 μF, 0.4-cm cuvettes). Cells were subsequently plated on MEF feeder layers (DR4 MEFs for puromycin or neomycin selection) in hESC medium supplemented with ROCK inhibitor for the first 24 hours, and then antibiotic selection was applied. Previously described 5iLA or 4iLA were assembled and applied as previously described (Theunissen et al., 2016). Reversion of primed hPSCs toward naive conditions was conducted on MEF or Matrigel coated plates in the specific media conditions indicated in figures. Although not essential, the use of ACTIVIN A and/or MEFs for the first 3 passages during the reversion process, accelerates transition to naive pluripotency in HENSM based platforms.

sec.title: Mouse naive and primed stem cell lines and cultivation
sec.p: Murine naive V6.5 ESCs (C57B6/129sJae) pluripotent cells were maintained and expanded in serum-free chemically defined N2B27-based media: 240 mL Neurobasal (ThermoFisher 21103049) and 240 mL of DMEM-F12 with HEPES (SIGMA D6421), 5 mL N2 supplement (Invitrogen; 17502048), 5 mL B27 supplement (Invitrogen; 17504044), 2 mM L-glutamine (Invitrogen), 1% nonessential amino acids (Invitrogen), 0.1 mM β-mercaptoethanol (Sigma), 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Invitrogen), 5 mg/ml BSA (Sigma). Naive 2i/LIF conditions for murine PSCs included 20 ng/ml recombinant human LIF (in-house made). Where indicated 2i was added: small-molecule inhibitors CHIR99021 (CH, 3 μM- Axon Medchem) and PD0325901 (PD, 1 μM – Axon Medchem 1408). Murine naive ESCs and iPSCs were expanded on gelatin-coated plates, unless indicated otherwise. Primed 129Jae EpiSC line (derived from E6.5 embryos) or C57BL6/129sJae EpiSC line (derived following in vitro priming of V6.5 mouse ESCs) were expanded in N2B27 with 12 ng/ml recombinant human bFGF (Peprotech) and 20 ng/ml recombinant Human ACTIVIN A (Peprotech). Murine EpiSC were expanded on feeder free Matrigel coated plates. Cell lines were routinely checked for Mycoplasma contaminations every month (LONZA – MYCOALERT KIT), and all samples analyzed in this study were not contaminated.

sec.title: METTL3 inducible mutant cell lines
sec.p: We engineered human WIBR3 hESC lines with inducible ablation of the expression of METTL3 (Figures 1A and 1B). This was obtained via introducing an exogenous METTL3 transgene under the regulation of Tet-OFF promoter (Liao et al., 2015), followed by CRISPR/Cas9 mediated ablation of both endogenous human METTL3 alleles (Figure 1A). Two resultant clones were validated for METTL3 expression only from the exogenous allele, which can be shut off by addition of DOX to the media (Tet-OFF-METTL3 lines) (Figure 1B). Generation of other mutants/reporter lines and their validation is detailed in the associated dataset deposited on Mendeley (https://dx.doi.org/10.17632/wfndbmjpyn.1). Human WIBR3 deltaPE-OCT4-GFP line (clone #1) previously described and used to generate results in (Theunissen et al., 2014), was found to be chromosomally abnormal, and thus was rederived and subcloned in the Hanna lab to obtain validated chromosomally normal cells on which reliable and coherent results could be obtained. X chromsome reporter WIBR2 hESC lines 29-8 and 29-9 (Theunissen et al., 2016) were simultaneously used in this study and yielded similar results.

sec.title: Small molecule compounds and cytokines used in small scale screens
sec.p: Small molecules and cytokines were supplemented as indicated in screening related figure legends: recombinant human BMP4 (10 ng/ml, Peprotech), BMPRi (LDN193189 0.3μM, Axon Medchem 1509), recombinant human IGF1 (10 ng/ml, Peprotech), Forskolin (FK, 10μM, TOCRIS), FGFR inhibitor PD173074 (0.1μM, TOCRIS), TGFRßi/ALK inhibitor A83-01 (0.3μM, Axon Medchem 1421), Kenopaullone (KP, 5μM, Sigma Aldrich), DOT1L inhibitor (SGC0946 0.5μM, SigmaAldrich SML1107), recombinant human SCF (10 ng/ml, Peprotech), SRCi CGP77675 (CGP77675 1μM – Axon Medchem 2097), TNKi (IWR1-endo 4μM - Axon Medchem 2510), Gamma Secretase / NOTCH pathway inhibitor (DBZ 0.35μM – Axon Medchem 1488), BRAFi (SB590885, 0.5μM, Axon Medchem 2504), ERK5i (BIX02189 5μM, Axon Medchem 1809), SHHi (RU-SKI43 3μM, Axon Medchem 2035), G9a inhibitor (BIX01294 0.5μM – Axon Medchem 1692), Medium with inhibitors was replaced every 24 hours. Doxycycline (DOX - SigmaAldrich D9891) was used at a final concentration of 2 μg/ml and refreshed every 48 hours upon media exchange. For exogenous L-GLUTAMINE withdrawal assay (“no GLUT assay”) (Carey et al., 2015), media indicated were used without addition of non-essential amino acids, without L-Glutamax, without added aKG, and without Matrigel/Geltrex as some of these components can introduce L-Glut precursors as well. Laminin511 (Biolamina) or Gelatin and irradiated feeders were used as coating material for no-GLUT assay. Flow cytometry measurement were conducted on FACS -CANTO II (BD), FACS ARIA-III (BD) or FACS-Celesta (BD). In all comparative FACS staining figures, we included measurements that were made on the same Flow cytometer per each figure, to avoid noise variance in signal strength that might originate when using different machines.

sec.title: ESC derivation from human blastocysts in HENSM conditions
sec.p: The use of human preimplantation embryos for ESC derivation was performed in compliance with protocols approved by LIS hospital ESCRO committee, Lis hospital Institutional review committee and Israeli National Ethics Committee (7/04-043) and following the acceptance of a written informed consent. The couples’ participation in the study was voluntary after signing informed consent forms and there was no monetary compensation for their embryo donation. Inner cell masses (ICMs) were isolated mechanically by laser-assisted micromanipulation from spare IVF embryos, at day 6-7 following fertilization. The intact ICM clumps were placed on a feeder cell layer of irradiation treated DR4 mouse embryonic fibroblasts and cultured in HENSM or HENSM-ACT media. Initial outgrowths of proliferating ESCs were evident by days 4-8, and were trypsinized into single cells, 6-10 days following ICM plating. The newly established cell lines were further propagated by 0.05% trypsin and then either frozen or used for further analysis. We were able to establish 3 newly derived stem cell lines in HENSM-ACT (n = 3 lines/ 7 blastocysts = 42% efficiency) and 2 new lines in HENSM conditions (n = 2 lines/ 7 blastocysts = 29% efficiency). The latter derivation efficiencies were at par to our derivations in primed or NHSM conditions when supplemented with ROCKi at the same IVF unit (previously described in Gafni et al. [2013]).

sec.title: Reprogramming of somatic cells and cell infection
sec.p: Virus-containing supernatants of the different reprogramming viruses: STEMCCA-OKSM polycistronic vector (DOX inducible and constitutive expression) was supplemented with the FUW-lox-M2rtTA virus (when necessary) and an equal volume of fresh culture medium for infection. For derivation of iPSCs directly from fibroblasts (and not from already established iPSC lines), fibroblasts were grown in the presence of DOX in HENSM conditions on Matrigel-coated plates until initial iPSC colonies were observed and subcloned. Generation of JH1 hiPSCs from human PBMCs was conducted by OSKM Sendai virus Cyto-Tune-iPS2.0 Kit according to manufacturer’s instructions but in HENSM conditions applied starting from day 4 of the reprogramming process.

sec.title: Differentiation of HENSM hPSCs to TSCs and PrE
sec.p: JHiPS, H1 and WIBR3 naive hPSCs expanded on HENSM were dissociated with TrypLE, and 2 X 10ˆ6 cells were seeded in Collagen IV (Sigma-Aldrich C5533) coated 10cm plates in HENSM medium and kept in the 20% O2 incubator. 2 days later the medium was changed to previously described TSC medium (Okae et al., 2018): DMEM:F12 supplemented with 0.2%FBS, 0.3% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich A9418), 0.1mM 2-mercaptoethanol (GIBCO 31350-010), 1% ITS-X (GIBCO, 51500), 1.5μM ascorbic acid (Sigma-Aldrich A8960), 50ng/ml EGF (Peprotech AF-100-15), 2μM CHIR99021 (Axon 1386), 0.5μM A83-01 (Axon 1421), 1μM SB431542 (Axon 1661), 0.8mM VPA (Sigma-Aldrich P4543), 5μM Y27632 (Axon 1683) and 0.5% Penicillin-Streptomycin. Medium was changed daily. When the flattened colonies reached 50%–70% confluency (around day 5 from the addition of TSC medium), they were passaged at 1:4 ratio. Homogeneous TSC cultures with rapid proliferation rate were established by third – fifth passage depending on the cell line background. The cells were passaged with TrypLE every 3-4 days at a ratio of 1:4 – 1:6. At passage 18 the cells were plated on coverslips and used for and stained with indicated antibodies for hTSC markers. Differentiation of HENSM naive WIBER3 hESCs naive into PrE was done as previously described (Linneberg-Agerholm et al., 2019). Briefly, cells were plated on feeders at 5 × 10ˆ4 per cmˆ2 in RACL medium [RPMI 1640 medium with GlutaMAX (61870044, GIBCO) with B27 minus insulin (A1895601, GIBCO) supplemented with 100 ng/ml ACTIVIN A, 3 μM CHIR and 10 ng/ml LIF] for 7 days (PrE) . RACL medium was changed every day. To achieve naive endodermal (nEND) cell expansion, after PrE cells reached confluency, they were passaged by dissociation using TrypleE and PBS 1:1 for 3 minutes and suspended with PBS. The cells were plated on 10 cm plate with feeders at in NACL medium (Neurobasal medium and DMEM/F12 1:1, N2B27 supplemented with 100ng/ml ACTIVIN A, 3 μM CHIR and 10 ng/ml LIF) every 4-7 days, supplemented with 10 μM ROCKi for the first 24 h (Linneberg-Agerholm et al., 2019).

sec.title: Mouse embryo micromanipulation and imaging
sec.p: Human naive pluripotent iPSCs in NHSM, NHSM+TNKi, HENSM, HENSM-ACT, tHENSM or 0HENSM were treated with 20 μM ROCKi the night before injection and trypsinized and microinjected into E2.5 BDF2 diploid morulas or aggregated with 2-Cell BDF2 embryos, and were subsequently allowed to develop in vitro until E3.5 (in KSOM medium or Continuous Single Culture-NX Complete medium (IrvineScientific)). Microinjection into E2.5 morulas placed in M16 medium under mineral oil was done by a flat-tip microinjection pipette. A controlled number of 4-8 cells were injected into the morulas. After injection, morulas were returned to KSOM media (Invitrogen) supplemented with 10-20 μm ROCKi for 4h, then transferred to KSOM without ROCKi and placed at 37°C until transferred to recipient females at E3.5. Ten to fifteen injected blastocysts were transferred to each uterine horn of 2.5 days post coitum pseudo-pregnant females. 120-150 embryos were obtained and transferred for each injection batch. Embryos were dissected at the indicated time points and imaged for GFP+ cell localization. The latter experiments were approved by Weizmann Institute IACUC (00330111-2) and by the Weizmann Institute Bioethics and ESCRO committee. In Toto confocal imaging of chimeric mouse embryos was conducted after that the embryos were removed from the uterus into Tyrode’s solution, the decidua removed and the embryo carefully isolated with yolk sac intact. Embryos were moved into a droplet of culture media on a paper filter attached to a coverslip with vacuum grease. Starting farthest away from the embryo, the yolk sac was gently peeled open and lightly pressed onto the paper filter, which has adherence qualities, to anchor the embryo to the filter. To expose the tissue of interest, the embryo can be stretched and lightly pressed onto the filter. After mounting the embryos, a glass-bottomed dish was placed over the embryos using vacuum grease drops for spacing. The dish was inverted, filled with culture media and placed in the imaging chamber on an inverted Zeiss confocal LSM700 microscope. No blinding or randomization was conducted when testing outcome of microinjection experiments. Mounted embryos were placed in a heat- and humidity-controlled chamber (37°C; 5% O2, 5% CO2 and 90% N2 gas mixture) on a motorized stage of an inverted Zeiss LSM700 confocal microscope. Images were acquired with a 20x/0.8 M27 lens with 0.5-0.6x digital zoom-out or 10x/0.3 Ph1 M27 lens with 0.5-0.6x digital zoom-out. For GFP detection, a 448- nm laser (30%–50% power) was used. Orange-Tracker (Molecular Probes, cat #C2927. Used at 20 μM) was excited by a 555-nm laser (30% power). Hoechst (Sigma, cat #B2261, used at 10 μg/ml) was excited by a 405-nm laser (40% power). RRX dyes were excited by 594 laser (20% power) and far-red dyes were excited by 647 laser (30% power). Images were acquired at 1024x1024 resolution. The thickness of z-slices appears in the relevant figure legends.

sec.title: Imaging, quantifications, and statistical analysis
sec.p: Images were acquired with D1 inverted microscope (Carl Zeiss, Germany) equipped with DP73 camera (Olympus, Japan) or with Zeiss LSM 700 inverted confocal microscope (Carl Zeiss, Germany) equipped with 405nm, 488nm, 555nm and 635 solid state lasers, using a 20x Plan-Apochromat objective (NA 0.8). All images were acquired in sequential mode. For comparative analysis, all parameters during image acquisition were kept constant throughout each experiment. Images were processed with Zen blue 2011 software (Carl Zeiss, Germany), and Adobe Photoshop CS4.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry analysis of mouse embryos
sec.p: Mouse embryos were harvested at the indicate time points, washed once in 1xPBS and fixated overnight in 4% PFA. Thereafter, embryos were washed three times in 1xPBS and dehydrated in sequential Ethanol dilutions. After standard paraffinization and embedding, tissue blocks were sectioned on a microtome at 6 μm thickness and mounted onto Superfrost plus slides (Thermo Scientific, Menzel-Glaser), dried at 38°C for 4 hours and stored at 4°C until further processing. Tissue sections were stained for following indicated antibodies: goat anti-GFP (Abcam ab6673), chicken anti-GFP (Abcam ab13970), rabbit anti-Numa (Abcam ab84680), mouse anti-human nuclei (Millipore MAB1281), mouse anti-TUJ1 (Covance MMS 435P), goat anti-SOX2 (R&D AF2018), goat anti-SOX17 (R&D AF1924). All secondary antibodies were used from Jackson ImmunoResearch including donkey anti-rabbit Biotin and Streptavidin-Cy3 for signal enhancement. For PFE-staining, sections were rehydrated, antigen retrieved in Sodium citrate buffer and pressure cooker, rinsed in PBS and treated with 0.3% H2O2 to reduce background staining. After permeabilization in 0.1% Triton X-100 in PBS three times for 2 min., samples were blocked in 10% normal donkey serum in PBS in humidified chamber for 20 min. at RT. Slides were then incubated in the appropriate primary antibody diluted in 1% BSA in 0.1% Triton X-100 at 4°C overnight. Sections were then washed three times (5 min each) in washing buffer (0.1% Triton X-100 in PBS), and incubated with appropriate fluorochrome-conjugated secondary antibodies diluted in 1% BSA in 0.1% Triton X-100 at RT for 1 h in the dark. For human cell specific NUMA staining, signal enhancement was performed by usage of Biotin-SP conjugated 2nd antibody for 30 min and subsequent incubation with Streptavidin-Cy3 antibody for 30 min. All sections were washed three times in washing buffer for 10 min each, counter stained with DAPI for 20 min, rinsed twice in washing buffer and mounted with Shandon Immuno-Mount (Thermo Scientific, 9990412). For OCT-staining, embryos were fixated o/n in 4% PFA at 4°C, washed three times in PBS for 10 min each and submerged first in 15% Sucrose/PBS and then 30% Sucrose o/n at 4°C. The day after, samples were subjected to increasing gradient of OCT concentration in Sucrose/PBS followed by embedding in OCT on dry ice and stored at −80°C until further processing. Cryoblocks were cut with LEICA CM1950 at 12 μm thickness and washed once with 1xPBS and incubated with 0.3% H2O2 for 20 min. After permeabilization with 0.1% Triton X-100 in PBS for 10 min., slides were again washed three times with 1xPBS for 2 min. each and blocked with blocked in 10% normal donkey serum in PBS in humidified chamber for 20 min. at RT. Antibody incubations were carried out analogously to PFE stainings. All images were collected on a Zeiss (Oberkochen, Germany) LSM700 confocal microscope and processed with Zeiss ZenDesk and Adobe Photoshop CS4 (Adobe Systems, San Jose, CA). For FACS analysis of mouse embryos, they were harvested and washed once in PBS. Thereafter, they were trypsinized in 0.05% trypsin/EDTA for 5 min and filtered through a cell strainer in MEF-medium before subjected to FACS analysis using FACS ARIA III analyzer and sorter system. Non-injected mouse embryos were used for proper gating and exclusion of auto-fluorescence.

sec.title: Luciferase activity assays
sec.p: WNT TOP-Flash reporter constructs (ten Berge et al., 2011) were used to determine the regulation pattern of WNT signaling activity and were electroporated into 0.5–3 × 10−6 cells along with the pRL-TK (Renilla) vector for normalization. Assays were performed 48 h later using the Dual-Glo Luciferase Assay System (Promega). The basal activity of the empty luciferase vector was set as 1.0.

sec.title: RT-PCR analysis
sec.p: Total RNA was isolated using Trizol (Ambion life technologies) and phenol-chloroform extraction. 1 μg of total RNA was reverse transcribed using a High-Capacity Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems) and ultimately re-suspended in 200 μl of water. Quantitative PCR analysis was performed in triplicate using 1/100 of the reverse transcription reaction in a Viia7 platform (Applied Biosystems). Normalization to ACTIN and GAPDH was done across all experiments, and data is presented in relevance to the indicated sample set as 1. Error bars indicate standard deviation of triplicate measurements for each measurement.

sec.title: Detection of miRNA expression in human ESCs/iPSCs
sec.p: RNA harvest was performed with miRNeasy Micro Kit (QIAGEN) and cDNA synthesized with miScript II RT kit (QIAGEN) using miScript HiFlex buffer. Real-time quantitative RT-PCR was performed using the miScript SYBR Green PCR kit (QIAGEN) and a ViiA 7 Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems). The primer concentration used was 1 μM in a final reaction volume of 10μl. Each reaction was performed in triplicate. The thermal cycling parameters were according to manufacturer orders (miScript SYBR green PCR kit).

sec.title: Human mitochondrial DNA PCR
sec.p: DNA was harvested with home-made lysis buffer (100 mM Tris pH8.0, 0.5 mM EDTA, 0.2% SDS, 200 mM NaCl, 200 ug/ml Proteinase K), precipitated with isopropanol and washed 1x with 70% Ethanol and finally eluted in 10 mM Tris-HCL pH 8, 0.1 mM EDTA. 50 ng template was used per reaction with SYBR Green Mastermix in ViiA 7 Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems). As endogenous control, UCNE expression was used and compared to amplification of human mitochondrial element DNA. Quantification was performed with delta/delta ct-method.

sec.title: Immunofluorescence staining
sec.p: Cells were grown for two days on glass coverslips (13mm 1.5H; Marienfeld, 0117530) fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde/phosphate buffer for 10 min at room temperature, washed three times with PBS, and permeabilized in PBS/0.1% Triton for 10 min. Cells were blocked with blocking solution (2% normal goat serum, 0.1% BSA in PBS/0.05% Tween) for 1h at RT and incubated with primary antibody diluted in blocking solution overnight at 4°C (Antibodies in this study have all been validated in the literature and by ourselves). Cells were then washed three times with PBS/0.05% Tween, incubated with secondary antibodies for 1 hour at room temperature, washed in PBS/0.05% Tween, counterstained with DAPI (1 μg/ml), washed again three times with PBS/Tween 0.05% and mounted with Shandon Immu-Mount (Thermo Scientific, 9990412), and imaged. All comparative experiments were done simultaneously. The following antibodies were use at the indicated dilutions: mouse anti-TRA-1-60 (Abcam ab16288, 1:500), mouse anti-TRA-1-81 (Abcam ab16289, 1:100), mouse anti-SSEA1 (Abcam ab16285, 1:100), mouse anti-SSEA4 (Abcam ab16287, 1:100), rat anti-SSEA3 (Abcam ab16286, 1:100), goat anti-NANOG (R/D AF1997, 1:50), rabbit anti-OCT3/4 (Santa Cruz SC9081, 1:400), mouse anti-OCT3/4 (Santa Cruz SC5279, 1:100), rabbit anti-KLF4 (Santa Cruz SC20691), mouse anti-ECAD (Abcam ab1416, 1:100), rabbit anti-NCAD (Abcam ab12221, 1:800), mouse anti-NR3B2 (R&D PPH670500, 1:1000), rabbit anti-TFE3 (SIGMA HPA023881, 1:500), rabbit anti-H3K27me3 (Abcam AB5603), goat anti-TFCP2L1 (RnD systems AF5726, 1:200), rabbit anti-NUMA (Abcam ab84680, 1:200), chicken anti-GFP (Abcam ab13970, 1:1000), rabbit anti-KLF17 (SIGMA HPA024629, 1:100), anti-TFAP2C (CSTH2320, 1:100, Cell Signaling), anti-STELLA (Santa Cruz, sc-376862, 1:100), anti-DNMT3L (Novus Biologicals, NPB2-27098, 1:200). All secondary antibodies were used from Jackson ImmunoResearch.

sec.title: Western blotting analysis
sec.p: Whole-cell protein extracts were isolated from human cells with conventional RIPA lysis buffer and protein concentration assayed by BCA kit (Thermo Scientific). Blocking was carried out in 10% skim milk in PBST for 1 h. Blots were incubated with the following antibodies in 5% BSA in PBST: KLF4 (AF3158; 1:200; R&D), OCT4 (H-134; 1:1,000; Santa Cruz), NANOG (397A; 1:1,000; Bethyl), METTL3 (A301-567A, 1:2000, Bethyl), HSP90beta (ab32568, 1:10000, Abcam), DNMT1 (ab87654, 1:1000, Abcam), GAPDH (ab181602, 1:10000, Abcam), ACTIN (ab6276, 1:10000, Abcam), UHRF1 (sc-373750, 1:1000, Santa Cruz), DGCR8 (10996-1-AP, 1:1000, Proteintech), P53 (D-01, courtesy from Varda Roter’s lab), β-catenin (sc-7963, 1:1000, Santa Cruz), TCF3 (CST2883, 1:1000, Cell Signaling), STAT3 (sc-482, 1:1000, Santa Cruz), KLF4 (sc-20691, 1:1000, Santa Cruz), RBPJ (C5 5313, 1:1000, Cell Signaling), TFAP2C (CSTH2320, 1:1000, Cell Signaling), STAT3 (sc-7993, 1:1000, Santa Cruz). Secondary antibodies were HRP-linked goat anti-mouse, goat anti-rabbit and rabbit anti-goat (1:10,000; Jackson). Blots were developed using SuperSignal West Pico Chemiluminescent Substrate (Thermo Scientific 34580).

sec.title: Whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) library preparation
sec.p: DNA was isolated from cells using the Quick-gDNA miniprep kit (Zymo). DNA (50ng) was then converted by bisulfite using the EZ DNA Methylation-Gold kit (Zymo). Libraries were prepared using the TruSeq kit (Illumina) and length distribution of each library was measured using the Bioanalyzer and product concentration was measured using Qubit Fluorometric Quantitation. For sequencing, the libraries, NextSeq 500/550 High Output v2 kit (150 cycles) was used. Data publicly deposited on GEO: GSE125555. Previously published human ICM WGBS data were taken from (Guo et al., 2014).

sec.title: Whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) analysis
sec.p: The sequencing reads were aligned to the human hg19 reference genome (UCSC, 2009), using a proprietary script based on Bowtie2. In cases where the two reads were not aligned in a concordant manner, the reads were discarded. Methylation levels of CpGs calculated by WGBS were unified. Mean methylation was calculated for each CpG that was covered by at least 5 distinct reads (X5). Average methylation level was calculating by taking the average over all covered X5 covered CpG sites in that genome.

sec.title: ChIP-seq library preparation
sec.p: Cells were crosslinked in formaldehyde (1% final concentration, 10 min at room temperature) or double crosslinked in DSG/formaldehyde (2mM DSG, 30 min at room temperature), then formaldehyde 1% final concentration, 10 min at room temperature) as detailed below per antibody, and then quenched with glycine (2.5M for 5 min at room temperature). Cells were lysed in 50 mM HEPES KOH pH 7.5, 140 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 10% glycerol, 0.5% NP-40 alternative, 0.25% Triton supplemented with protease inhibitor at 4 °C (Roche, 04693159001) for 10 min, and later centrifuged at 950g for 10 min. Supernatant was discarded and pellet was resuspended in RIPA-1 (0.2% SDS, 1 mM EDTA, 0.1% DOC, 140 mM NaCl and 10 mM Tris-HCl) with protease inhibitor. Cells were then fragmented with a Branson Sonifier (model S-450D) at −4 °C to size ranges between 200 and 800 bp and centrifugation at max speed for 10 min. Supernatant lysate was extracted and diluted with RIPA 2-3-fold (0.1% SDS, 1 mM EDTA, 0.1% DOC, Triton 1%, 140 mM NaCl and 10 mM Tris-HCl). Small amount of lysate were saved for whole cell extract at this point. Antibody was pre-bound by incubating with Protein-G Dynabeads (Invitrogen 10004D) in blocking buffer (PBS supplemented with 0.5% TWEEN and 0.5% BSA) for 1 h at room temperature. Washed beads were added to the lysate for incubation as detail per antibody. Samples were washed five times with RIPA buffer, twice with RIPA buffer supplemented with 500 mM NaCl, twice with LiCl buffer (10 mM TE, 250mM LiCl, 0.5% NP-40, 0.5% DOC), once with TE (10Mm Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 1mM EDTA), and then eluted in 0.5% SDS, 300 mM NaCl, 5 mM EDTA, 10 mM Tris HCl pH 8.0. Eluate was incubated treated sequentially with RNaseA (Roche, 11119915001) for 30 min in 37°C and proteinase K (NEB, P8102S) for 2 h in 37°C and de-crosslinked in 65 °C for 8 h. DNA was purified with Agencourt AMPure XP system (Beckman Coulter Genomics, A63881). Libraries of cross-reversed ChIP DNA samples were prepared according to a modified version of the Illumina Genomic DNA protocol, as described previously (Rais et al., 2013). Treatment per antibody: KLF17 – double crosslinked, cell amount: 30 million, antibody: 6ug HPA024629 - atlas antibodies, incubation time: overnight. KLF4 – crosslinked, cell amount: 30 million, antibody: 10ug AF3158- R&D systems, incubation time: overnight, comment: This is a mouse Klf4 antibody that was verified to work on human using IF staining. NANOG – crosslinked, cell amount:30 million, antibody: 6ug AF1997- R&D systems, incubation time: overnight. OCT4 – crosslinked, cell amount:30 million, antibody: 10ug SC8628 Santa-Cruz, incubation time: overnight. SOX2 – crosslinked, cell amount:30 million, antibody: 10ug AF2018- R&D systems, incubation time: overnight. TFAP2c – crosslinked, cell amount:30 million, antibody: 5ug sc-8977 Santa-Cruz, incubation time: overnight. H3K27ac – crosslinked, cell amount:5 million, antibody: 5ug ab4729 Abcam, incubation time: 6 hours.

sec.title: ChIP-seq analysis
sec.p: We analyzed Chip-seq data of the following DNA-binding proteins: NANOG, SOX2, OCT4, KLF4, KLF17, TFAP2C, H3K27AC, in HENSM based or primed conditions, with replicates or triplicates for each antibody per single condition. For alignment and peak detection, we used bowtie2 software to align reads to human hg19 reference genome , with default parameters. We identified enriched intervals of all measured proteins using MACS version 1.4.2-1. We used sequencing of whole-cell extract as control to define a background model. Duplicate reads aligned to the exact same location are excluded by MACS default configuration. The number of peaks in Primed conditions were in-par with previous publications (e.g., PMID 25409831, PMID 19829295, Table S6). Peaks that were observed in at least two replicates were kept for further analysis. Peaks were assigned to genes using Homer software (Table S6). Motif enrichment analysis was performed using Homers findmotifsgenome.pl, with parameter -size 50 (Table S5). Significance of overlap between TF targets was calculated using Fisher exact test (Figure 6H).

sec.title: RNA-seq library preparation
sec.p: Total RNA was isolated from indicated cell lines and extracted from Trizol pellets by chloroform-phenol extraction protocol, then cleaned using Ribo-Zero (Illumina Ribo-Zero Plus rRNA Depletion Kit, ID-20037135) or Poly-A (Dynabeads mRNA DIRECT Kit (Invitrogen),ID-61012) depletion Kits. Cleaned RNA was next utilized for RNA-Seq by ScriptSeq Preparation Kit v2 (Illumina) according to manufacturer’s instruction.

sec.title: RNA-seq analysis
sec.p: hESCs grown in naive and primed conditions, from different cell lines (LIS41, LIS49, WIBR2, WIBR3, H1, H9, HUES64) were used for RNA-seq analysis. Overall 44 samples were sequenced using poly-A single-end strategy, and 19 samples were sequenced using ribo-zero paired-end strategy. STAR software version 2.5.2b was used to align reads to human GRCh38 reference genome (2013), using the following flags:–outFilterMultimapNmax 1–outReadsUnmapped Fastx–twopassMode Basic–outSAMstrandField intronMotif. Read count values were estimated with HTSeq V0.7.2 software over all aligned reads using GRCh38 general feature format (GFF), with the following flags: -a 10 -s no -t exon -i gene_id. Mitochondrial and ribosomal genes were filtered out. Genes with a sum count across all samples < 10, were filtered out as well. The filtering was done independently in each analysis, therefore the number of genes included may change, as it is dependent on the samples that were included for that analysis. Count values were normalized using R DESeq2 V1.26 software, and corrected for batch effects using R Limma V3.42. Variance stabilizing transformation was performed to all datasets as well. Dataset analysis and plotting was performed by R V3.6. Sample correlation was performed using Spearman method. Hierarchical clustering was carried out using “complete” or “Ward.D2” methods. Heatmap plots were first Z-scored by sample to better emphasize gene separation. Differentially expressed genes between Naive and Primed samples were performed by the following parameters: log2(Fold change) > 2 or log2(Fold change) < −2, and adjusted p value < 0.1. RNA-GSEA was performed on the vectorized log-foldchanges of all statistically significant differential expressed genes between the naive and primed conditions and compared to geneset from (Yan et al., 2013; Tyser et al., 2020)
. Previously published RNA-seq datasets were taken from (Theunissen et al., 2016; Theunissen et al., 2014 and Takashima et al., 2014). GSEA utilized the R packages “gage” and “fgsea”.

sec.title: ATAC-seq library preparation
sec.p: Cells were trypsinized and counted, 50,000 cells were centrifuged at 500g for 3 min, followed by a wash using 50 μL of cold PBS and centrifugation at 500g for 3 min. Cells were lysed using cold lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 10 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl2 and 0.1% IGEPAL CA-630). Immediately after lysis, nuclei were spun at 500g for 10 min using a refrigerated centrifuge. Next, the pellet was resuspended in the transposase reaction mix (25 μL 2 × TD buffer, 2.5 μL transposase (Illumina) and 22.5 μL nuclease-free water). The transposition reaction was carried out for 30 min at 37°C and immediately put on ice. Directly afterward, the sample was purified using a QIAGEN MinElute kit. Following purification, the library fragments were amplified using custom Nextera PCR primers 1 and 2 for a total of 12 cycles. Following PCR amplification, the libraries were purified using a QIAGENMinElute Kit and sequenced.

sec.title: ATAC-seq analysis
sec.p: Reads were aligned to hg19 human genome using Bowtie2 with the parameter -X2000 (allowing fragments up to 2 kb to align). Duplicated aligned reads were removed using Picard MarkDuplicates tool with the command REMOVE_DUPLICATES = true. To identify chromatin accessibility signal we considered only short reads (≤120bp) that correspond to nucleosome free region. To detect and separate accessible loci in each sample, we used MACS version 1.4.2-1 with–call-subpeaks flag (PeakSplitter version 1.0). To generate the final ATAC loci of naive and primed conditions, we selected peaks that appear in the majority of the replicates of each condition, i.e., 3 out of 4 naive samples, and 2 out of 3 primed samples. In vivo developmental ATAC-seq datasets were taken from (Wu et al., 2018).

sec.title: Enhancer identification
sec.p: H3K27ac peaks were detected using MACS version 1.4.2-1 and merged for each condition (naive and primed) using bedtools merge command. All ATAC peaks were filtered to include only peaks which co-localized with the merged H3K27ac peaks in at least one condition. Finally, peaks that co-localized with promoter or exon regions based on hg19 assembly were filtered out. Finally, we were left with defined genomic intervals which we annotated as enhancers.

sec.title: SNP score calculation from WGS
sec.p: SNP score calculation was done as previously described (Bar et al., 2017). Briefly, we downloaded WGS data for H1 and H9 cell lines from the SRA database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra). The files were extracted using SRAtools and aligned to the hg19 reference genome using BWA. SAMtools was used to convert from SAM to BAM. We then detected polymorphisms with the same pipeline as described previously for RNA-seq (without filtering for FPKM). In order to test if genomic SNPs are properly detected in the RNA-seq analysis, we extracted SNPs from exons of control pluripotent genes and calculated the average percentage of overlapping SNPs between WGS and RNA-seq of the appropriate H1 and H9 samples. In order to test if there is a difference in the existence of genomic SNPs between imprinted genes governed by maternal and paternal gDMR, we extracted the SNPs located at exons of imprinted genes from WGS of H1 and H9 cell lines and then calculated the percentage of genes with genomic SNPs in each group. We used a chi-square test, which confirmed that the bias was not significant.

sec.title: Quantifying X:A allelic ratio
sec.p: X:A allelic ration was done as previously described (Bar et al., 2019). Briefly, to generate a quantifiable score of allelic expression across the X chromosome, we developed the X:Autosomes (X:A) allelic ratio. For this we first counted the number of biallelic SNPs in each chromosome. Since our analysis is based on expressed SNPs, this sum is expected to be dependent on the number of genes in the chromosome. Therefore, to overcome this bias we generated a normalized SNP sum by dividing the SNP sum with the number of known genes in each chromosome. We validated that the average of this normalized SNP sum was similar across all autosomes. Next, for each sample we calculated the ratio of normalized SNP sum of X chromosome and the average normalized SNP sum of autosomes:NS (normalized sum)=Sum(biallelic SNPs) / No. of genes in chromosomeX : A allelic ratio = X chromosome−NS / Average (Autosome−NS)By comparing the normalized sum of X and autosomes within each sample, we avoid potential biases which are due to coverage and batch issues. Samples with very low normalized SNP sums in autosomes (for example haploid samples or their diploid genetic match which are completely homozygous), were discarded from this analysis.

sec.title: Transposon expression profiling
sec.p: TE profiling was performed as previously described (Theunissen et al., 2016). For repetitive sequences an D. Trono lab curated version of the Repbase database was used (fragmented LTR and internal segments belonging to a single integrant were merged). TEs counts were generated using the multiBamCov tool from the bedtools software. TEs which did not have at least one sample with 20 reads (after normalizing for sequencing depth) were discarded from the analysis. TEs overlapping exons were also removed from the analysis. Normalization for sequencing depth and differential gene expression analysis was performed using Voom as it has been implemented in the limma package of Bioconductor. A gene (or TE) was considered to be differentially expressed when the fold change between groups was bigger than 2 and the p value was smaller than 0.05. A moderated paired t test (as implemented in the limma package of R) was used to test significance. P values were corrected for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg’s method. Single cell RNA-Seq data was downloaded from GEO (GSE36552). Data was mapped and processed as explained above. When merging with in-house RNA-Seq, only TEs which were expressed in both datasets were used. To be considered expressed, the TE needed to have at least as many reads across all samples as samples existed in each dataset. Correspondence between naive/primed ESCs and single cell expression data from human embryonic stages w`s also done as described before (Theunissen et al., 2016). For every cell state we perform a statistical test to find the genes (or TEs) that have a different expression level compared to the other cell states (Yan et al., 2013). For this we use a moderated F-test (comparing the interest group against every other) as implemented in the limma package of Bioconductor. For a gene (or TE) to be selected as expressed in a specific cell state it needs to have a significant p value (< 0.05 after adjusting for multiple testing with the Benjamini and Hochberg method) and an average fold change respective to the other cell states greater than 10. Note that with this approach a gene (or TE) can be marked as expressed in more than one cell state. Once we have the genes (or TEs) that are expressed in a specific cell state we ask if those genes are more expressed in primed or in naive. For that we see how many of the genes are up (or down) regulated in the primed/naive pairwise comparison. For a gene to be considered differentially expressed it needs to have a p value (after multiple testing correction with the Benjamini and Hochberg method) lower than 0.05 and a fold change greater than 2.
